utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. And I'd like to thank you once again for having enabled me to use a bit more time to overcome my health problems. I will try to make up for the time lost with this penultimate witness, who also appears here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you tell Their Honours what your first and last name is.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Desimir Garovic, a retired general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to hear your first and last name. Can you please tell Their Honours your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 14th of April, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately I have to deal with a few issues before I turn directly to this witness' report. First of all, briefly of course, I have to deal with a large set of documents I received from the Prosecutor. These documents have to do with a stage in his life, and perhaps he can briefly explain a few things to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you are a retired general. What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During the time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in particular at the time when the events discussed here were taking place and back in 1991, what were you then?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was in Banja Luka and I was a lieutenant colonel. I commanded an artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were in Banja Luka. What do you mean by that? How did it come about that you were in Banja Luka at the time?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: At that time I lived in Banja Luka, working in that garrison, and my family was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long before 1991 did you live in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: As of January 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite a number of years, then. You were sent there on duty by the army of the then country. You didn't know how long you were supposed to stay there.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I was employed by the Yugoslav People's Army and the exigencies of the service required that I be in the garrison in Banja Luka. However, I didn't know how long I was to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also had an apartment.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an apartment in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I left Banja Luka after a presidency decision which had to do with us moving to the territory of the FRY in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to Banja Luka after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I did, towards the end of August when conditions were such that I could collect my belongings from the apartment and transport them to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then with your friends and acquaintances? Was there anything taking place?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: It is customary that once one leaves a garrison there is usually a farewell party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell too much on it and waste too much time. I think there are over 100 pages here that can be discussed. But tell me this, please: At that time what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: No. In 1992, I was a lieutenant. Just before the war I was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you become a lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever command a tank unit comprising 50 tanks?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: No. In my unit there was no such weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on that. I just wanted to ask for your assistance concerning some matters pertaining to the characteristics of artillery weapons and whether you know anything about craters, compasses and other things requiring certain mathematical calculations. I don't want to ask you anything about your curriculum vitae and your professional career in the JNA from this point on. Can you tell Their Honours, what was your rank at that time? You've explained already but perhaps you can repeat.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when I was retired my rank was that of a major general. My duty was chief of the educational directorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your immediate speciality? Perhaps you can explain.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: My speciality is artillery, ground artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that, does that mean that you have certain knowledge concerning behaviour of artillery, weaponry, aircraft bombs, and similar weapons?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I even taught concerning the use of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On this Defence's request you compiled a written report in which you explained the use and effect of artillery weapons. In the same paper you also explain certain characteristics of aircraft bombs. What was your basis for the report?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I based my report on the existing literature in possession of the army of Yugoslavia and the former JNA; then based on my previous personal experience and the experience and knowledge and skills I gained by studying other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the report you also state that you had in mind certain incidents when doing your analyses, incidents encompassed by this Prosecution's indictment against General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your report, the one bearing the number DD00-4582, referring to the incidents of shelling and dropping of airbombs? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That report is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us that this is the report compiled by you, judging by the cover page that you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like this document, DD00-4582, have admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us turn now to a few things concerning some data about the 120-millimetre mortar M-75. It was also a part of your analyses. It is on page 8 of your report in B/C/S. In the English version, it is page 6. I wanted to ask you a few questions regarding that. Can you explain to Their Honours something about the characteristics of that particular mortar. How does one move such a calibre weapon from one firing position to another?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Any movement of such a weapon from one place to another is done by using engines, vehicles, having in mind the number of people belonging to its crew and its sheer weight. There is no other way to transport that weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When is such a weapon used, or rather, when it is being used, what impact does it have upon the surface it was placed on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That particular place from which a 120-millimetre mortar fired from had to have been prepared. The base plate has to be pushed into the ground and certain canals have to be dug out inside which the legs can be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of traces are left on the surface?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The traces of the plate and the legs, of course, and this usually covers an area of some 5 to 6 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One last thing on that topic. Does such a weapon, or rather, can it be placed on a stone surface?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: According to our rules, it is forbidden to place such a mortar on a stone surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you not to rush with your answers. Wait for the cursor to stop and allow for a small pause after my question.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why is that not allowed?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A stone surface is hard. It doesn't provide for any further operation of firing. The mortar would simply bounce off the surface and wouldn't be much use if trying to fire again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your report does not include any type of information or assessment regarding artillery weapons, or the artillery weapon called Nora. I wanted to ask whether you know anything about that weapon system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Judge Harhoff has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Before we leave the mortars and move on to the Nora weapon, I would like to ask a few additional questions regarding the mortars. First of all, 120-millimetre mortar, what is the total weight of that weapon? The indications here are not entirely clear in your report, at least as I can see. How much is -- what is the weight of the plate of a 120-millimetre mortar, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have cited the weight of the weapon when it is in a combat position. Also, undercarriage is being used for transporting the weapon, and the total weight of it is 300 kilometres [sic] on march. The weight of individual components varies. For example, the base plate is nearly 80 kilometres, and if you allow me, I may consult the rules and therefore provide you with accurate figures. However, an ordinary person, an individual, is unable to carry it from one place to another. Not a single part of the mortar can be carried by an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Let me just, for the record, say that the indication of the weight, I suppose, should be kilogrammes. It has been translated as kilometres, but I suppose this is a mistake. So the base plate itself weighs 80 kilogrammes, approximately. That means that two persons could lift it from a car or a truck down onto the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mortar is being towed. It's coupled to a motor vehicle. It is not being carried. It is not loaded onto a truck, it's being towed from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please forgive us, General. I think you might wish to explain to us just how a mortar works. The Bench is not composed of experts in artillery weapons. So you say that a mortar is being pulled on wheels, I suppose, after a truck or a vehicle. Then what happens when it arrives to the firing location? Can it then -- I suppose it has to be lowered so as to stand directly on the ground. How is that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, along with the mortar that you can see on the picture, there is a sort of undercarriage or carriage that has two wheels. The mortar is mounted on this carriage and this whole assembly is a kind of trailer that can be coupled with a motor vehicle and transported to another location. Upon the arrival to the location, this carriage is detached and disconnected and the mortar remains as shown in the picture, and then it is prepared for operation. A 120-millimetre mortar is not loaded onto a vehicle. It has its own structure that allows it to be towed as a trailer attached to a motor vehicle. And that applies to all mortars that I used all around the world. They are structured in that way. They have rubber wheels and they have a shackle that is used to be attached to a vehicle. I hope I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have been perfectly clear, but still I need to understand and to see for myself how it works. And the reason I'm asking these questions is that in this case we have been dealing a lot with the possible firing positions of mortars, so this is why the Bench needs to become a little more familiar through your expertise about just how it works in practice. Now, I suppose the base plate is standing directly on the ground immediately before firing the mortar, and the legs as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the carriage is detached from the mortar, it is moved to 10 or 15 metres. It's a separate component upon which the mortar is loaded and fixed. The carriage has no effect on the combat operation. It is just used for transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. So when the mortar is then fired, what sort of traces would be left on the ground once the mortar is removed? Would that be traces from the pressure of the explosion into the ground or would it be gunpowder or smoke or remnants of powder? What would you find on the ground? How would you be able to see that a mortar was fired from here? What would you look for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an imprint of the base plate. It's circular. And it remains in the ground depending on the hardness of the surface. So this imprint can be 10 to 15 centimetres deep and that's the only reliable trace indicating that this is the position from which a 120-millimetre mortar was fired. This trace on the surface is 60 to 70 centimetres in diameter. So it is clearly shown on the ground, indicating that a mortar was fired from that particular place, and that's the only reliable information that can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you said that if a mortar was fired from directly on a rock, that would be senseless because the weapon, as a result of the explosion, would bounce off the ground and be destroyed. So you would normally fire a mortar from a ground that would allow some sort of, what should I say, flexibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the ground is dry, then would you still be -- dry and hard, but still it would be earth, but dry earth, would you still be able to see an imprint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be fired from any kind of surface, soft ground or hard ground. This kind of surface is not hard enough to prevent the use of the mortar. Only in the case of a rocky surface, that can present even danger for the crew operating the mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But say if I were to fire a 120-millimetre mortar from a football field. I suppose we all have a sort of sense of how soft the ground is on a football field. In that case you would say, if I understand you correctly, that the mortar would leave an imprint in the grass of somewhere between 10 and 15 centimetres of depth, when you remove the base plate. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have a football pitch, that would be the imprint left. Other kinds of surfaces are harder than a football pitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly. And so my question is: If you then move to a place where the ground is very dry and therefore quite hard, my question is: Would you still be able to see an imprint, perhaps only of a few centimetres, or would there be any imprint left at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The depth would be 2 to 3 centimetres, but of course it would be visible and one could deduce that that mortar was used there. But I keep repeating, if we are talking about dirt or soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood this. Would there be any imprints left from the legs of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What would they look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As if you put a stick into the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right. And would there be gunpowder or smoke or burnt-off areas around the base plate in the grass or in the vegetation, if there is any, or would there only be the imprint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the imprint. Gunpowder gases, given the nature of the firing and the elevation, are not present anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This applies to the 120-millimetre mortar. What is the imprint left by an 82-millimetre mortar? Are they the same, just smaller?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are smaller, but as far as the shape and other characteristics are concerned, they are the same. They are just smaller. And that is how you can tell the difference between the 82-millimetre and the 120-millimetre, according to the size and the shape of the imprint found on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garovic, as a follow-up to the question asked by His Honour Judge Harhoff, if we have a mortar firing from a certain position and it needs to be shifted to another location, a closer one or a further one, is it necessary for it to be given appropriate towing? As you said, it was brought to the location using what?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of motor vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: In our vocabulary we call it a truck. These were typical JNA trucks, JAP 150 -- sorry, FAP 150 and 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When they move in the field --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: They leave traces of motor vehicle passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When they arrive there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please observe a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, the tow-truck leaves tracks when it arrives to the location, so it leaves the tracks and traces on the grass and in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if it were to change location and go to another position, the mortar is again attached to the truck.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is part of the base plate, or any other element for that matter, is embedded at this particular location? Or, in other words, is it always put on the grass directly or in the field? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: In order for the mortar to become operational, preparations have to be made for the location where the base plate is going to be put. One part is embedded into the earth in order to stabilise it for firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a little bit concerned about the time that has already elapsed. Can you tell us briefly, please, what do you know about Nora?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Nora is an artillery weapon in the arsenal of the JNA. It falls into the howitzer gun category of weapons and its range is 24 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be sufficient. Can you tell me, because I would like to hear that as well: Judge Harhoff asked you whether it was possible for two men to lift 80 kilogrammes, if I remember correctly. You said that the carriage weighs about that.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, about 80 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could two men, soldiers - those are mainly 19-year-olds - lift 80 kilogrammes?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they can, but they cannot carry it too large a distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the carriage was normally parked at what distance from the firing position?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Five to 10 metres, depending on the configuration of the ground, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So practically it is simply detached. It is not being lifted.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: It's being just detached from the mortar and it serves only for the transportation and towing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the chapter entitled "The Rules of Use of Firing Weapons for Direct Support," which is on page 11 in the B/C/S version and page 8 in the English version, you explained this topic in great detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garovic, I'm not going to go back on everything that you wrote down, except for a few details that I will address later on, but I would like to hear certain explanations from you relating to the issues raised here and it will be up to the Chamber to arrive at final conclusions. What is not included in your report is the description of how a mortar and artillery unit is being deployed in the course of a combat operation. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A mortar battery in combat operation is deployed in the following way: Mortars are being placed at firing positions which is far from the confrontation line, 2 to 4 kilometres. Part of the units, which is to say one or two men, are deployed at observation points --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for my next question. You gave me the answer. Now please wait for me to pose the next question. First of all, when you speak about firing positions and observation points or observers, does the same arrangement apply to direct and indirect fire? I'm not going to seek explanation for either of these notions. It's already well known. So does this arrangement exist in both instances?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose position is an observer or spotter?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: He is deployed as part of his own force, as close to the line of confrontation as possible. In principle, it is between 500 and 1.500 metres away from the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Facing the firing position of his own forces which are to his rear?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What would be the role of an observer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no objection, obviously, with respect to the expertise this witness can offer in this subject of observation and observers being deployed by military formations. However, as Mr. Tapuskovic has said now with respect to two subjects, this information, this evidence, is not contained in the expert's report and one would have thought that if Mr. Tapuskovic wants to lead this evidence, that such instructions would have been given to the expert at the outset of his work on the report. Now, of course the Prosecution is aware of these issues, and they are issues in this case. However, the purpose of an expert filing his report or her report is to provide a copy of that report 30 days prior to the testimony of that expert, and that's contained in Rule 94 bis, because some of the analysis and some of the expertise given on the stand or given in the report need to be assessed and examined efficiently by the Prosecution and therefore the 30-day limit is given. Putting new areas that are not contained in the report to the witness and for the witness to now be giving expert opinions and conclusions on these issues, in the Prosecution's submission, impacts on the fairness of the proceedings to some extent. And I also take the opportunity to pre-empt or to mention that the Prosecution has filed a motion on similar considerations with respect to the last witness tomorrow. I think this was filed or will be filed today on similar issues. I just would like to point that out, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have heard the objection, Mr. Tapuskovic. You are now leading evidence on matters not in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, there are still some issues pending and they remain so after this -- after the compiling of this report. I wanted to hear from the witness some of his general opinion as to the activity of certain types of artillery weapons as regards the type of crater, the use of sights, and so on and so forth. All of that he put in the context of events from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva, the Chamber is not with you on this point. We believe that these matters arise naturally from the expert's report and these are matters on which one would expect questions to be asked. I believe that you have taken too literally the requirement that matters dealt with in examination-in-chief in relation to an expert should be contained in the report. That is so, generally speaking, but where matters arise incidentally from the expertise of the expert, I see no objection to it. Proceed, and please remember the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the only thing on my mind currently. However, we spent quite some time on one particular issue and there were questions put by the Judges. I am compelled to use only those documents that have previously been used by the Prosecutor. All the documents that I present to the witness will be of that type. These will only be Prosecution documents. I will not use any additional ones. I will only seek clarification on certain of those documents. Later on there will be some other issues that may raise questions on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this, Witness: What is the role of an observer?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: An artillery observer is tasked with monitoring the situation on the battlefield and the situation with the enemy. He needs to make certain assessments as to the activity of the enemy and inform his superior of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to dwell too much on that, but when it comes to firing from a mortar, especially a 120-millimetre mortar, at what stage is the observer's role crucial with both direct and indirect firing?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: On his superior's approval, the artillery observer can carry out corrections after the first projectile had been fired at the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you analysed another witness report - this witness was examined by the Prosecutor - and since you are expertise in that field, what does an entered target mean?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I have encountered that term for the first time in that very text. In my entire career I have never seen such a term. As far as I can understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. But if one says "entered target," what does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: It tells me that all of the targets or a part of the targets chosen by an artillery is then -- their coordinates set up on the sighting devices. Therefore, at any given moment fire can be opened against such targets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: We believe the correct term is a presighted target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that someone has entered or presighted a target three months in advance and you come three months later, put in a charge and hit the target without any errors?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That is not possible. In order to fire a projectile concerning the weapons from the JNA's arsenal, you can hit the target only given that it was presighted immediately prior to that. It is not possible to presight a target and fire at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I want to move further now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I would like to comment because the English term used, "presighted," has appeared twice and the first time -- well, I'm also listening in B/C/S as I speak in French. It's not coordinate presighted, because Mr. Tapuskovic used another term in B/C/S which means predetermined, predetermined target. So I think that the -- that would be the more appropriate term based on the word used in B/C/S and based on the meaning that was given by the expert. So I just wanted to make this point to avoid any misunderstanding when the transcript is reread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Predetermined, then. Does the interpreter agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To presight the weapon, the interpreters believe, means to set the coordinates for the target in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just add that since Mr. Tapuskovic referred to the expert evidence of Mr. Higgs and Mr. Higgs' official report, the term is prerecorded sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have a number of variances. Prerecorded, presighted, predetermined.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I just think we have to agree that all of the various interpretation booths use the same term because, of course, today's expert is listening in B/C/S, as well as Mr. Tapuskovic. So we have to be sure we're using the same term that was used by Mr. Higgs, because one of the words used in B/C/S does not correspond to the meaning of prerecorded. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the substance of the matter is quite clear. I don't think we need to trouble the interpreters any further on this. Please continue. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could I please ask you what you think the appropriate translation is in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prerecorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the most important thing concerning the flight of a projectile once it was fired, something that cannot be prerecorded, presighted, or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Concerning all of the elements important to the flight of a projectile, the weather conditions are the most important. They have a significant impact on the flight characteristics and pattern of that particular projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of all of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. You had earlier asked the witness a question about a mortar being set three months before. I wasn't clear as to the answer that was given. And I would ask you whether this WAS actually based on evidence in the case. Would you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try to find that reference in the Higgs report so as to make that issue perfectly clear. For your sake, I wanted to say that it was Higgs' belief that because of the type of conflict and the situation in Sarajevo, it was easy to have prerecorded sights all over town. The attackers knew where the main assembly points are and where civilians would be. If one wanted to use a single projectile while at the same time causing the maximum damage, then this target would have been the best target. It was Mr. Higgs' opinion that it sufficed to prerecord a sight, since one knew in advance where the civilians would be, and then what one needed to do was only to pull the trigger, causing the damage. This was Mr. Higgs' opinion in T558. That is why I'm asking this expert whether there is such a possibility that someone a month ago or a year ago prerecords a sight, lets some time elapse, then pull the trigger and hit the very same target he had fired on a year before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the witness' answer was no; isn't that so? Yes. And would you explain why, in your view, that was not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The impact of various factors on the flight of the projectile is such that even one hour before a round is fired, the calculated elements are incorrect to a certain extent, and they particularly -- the weather conditions and ballistic conditions affect the flight of the projectile. The weather in Sarajevo from the point of view of use of artillery, it's characteristic of a mountain area. The wind speed, wind direction, they affect the flight of the projectile to such an extent that it is impossible for the round to hit the target precisely, even if we calculated all the elements. Quite simply put: An hour is a long time period for the artillery fired to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the hypothesis put to you was actually three months, so that the -- it would be even more inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite inaccurate, inaccurate to a very high degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's not so much that it couldn't be done but that the projectile -- the accuracy would not be guaranteed. In fact, the accuracy would be quite compromised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I suppose atmospheric, the pressure of the air also has an influence, aside from the wind speed and wind direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Atmospheric pressure affects the density of the atmosphere. If the atmosphere is more dense, then there is a greater resistance and that would affect the range and the flight of the round, even if you fire them using the same firing elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the type of target, a mountain, for example, or a hill, would it be possible that the target be prerecorded, let's say, three months ahead of time with the same weather conditions and then be just as accurate? In other words, if the information was prerecorded three months ahead of time, including the weather, the temperature, the air pressure, et cetera, and three months later if the data is identical, then would it be possible to tier precisely? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is impossible to have firing conditions that would be so identical that after a period of three months you could say the conditions now are exactly the same. Even the rounds that are being fired vary in weight and in other characteristics and that affects the accuracy of the fire, too. There are many parameters that affect the accuracy of artillery fire. These parameters make it impossible to prerecord coordinates for the targets in order to achieve accurate fire after a long time period. As a teacher, a long-time teacher of artillery units, this is something that I have not encountered in theory or in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're on this topic, is it possible, then, to plan things three months, a year, or even two days in advance and then to have this element, this thing that was termed the prerecorded target, to make it possible for the first shell to hit exactly where it was intended?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: What I said about three months applies equally to one hour. Because Sarajevo is in the mountainous region - I lived in Sarajevo - and the atmospheric conditions change within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to speed things up a bit. Could you please tell me: If we're talking about an armed conflict, could you please explain to the Judges, how do the warring factions -- what do they do after artillery fire? Do they change their positions, do they move artillery pieces after artillery fire? And are artillery pieces moved at all from one position to another?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the warring factions try to locate some key pieces, artillery pieces of the other units, in order to fire on them and destroy them as soon as possible. And artillery of course is of particular interest and that is why artillery units often move from one firing position to another two or three times a day, sometimes even more, in order to avoid enemy fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another topic. Could you please tell the Judges, when we're talking about a 120-millimetre mortar, as far as you know based on your experience, at what distance can you hear such a mortar being fired, a 120-millimetre mortar, if we're talking about a person with the average hearing?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on my long experience, because I fired this type of mortar, an ordinary person with the average hearing can hear it from a distance of 5 to 6 kilometres at least, and a person with extraordinarily good hearing can hear it from a longer distance of about 40 kilometres from the place where the mortar was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says 40 kilometres here and the witness said 10 kilometres, 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But let me be more specific. Is it possible at all not to hear this from a distance of about 5 to 6 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: One must hear the sound of a mortar being fired from that distance, 5 to 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you briefly document P888. It is an information report, a preliminary report, filed by Mr. Higgs. It's been admitted into evidence. The last page of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we move on, could I just ask one clarifying question to the witness. What is the sound you hear, actually? Is it the explosion or is it the whistling sound of the trajectory?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, I insisted on the sound of the mortar being fired, when the mortar is being fired. Of course, you are entitled to ask the witness the question, but I insisted in my question that -- about the sound of the mortar being fired. The sound of a round in flight is something different, but we will get to that. But we are now talking about the sound when a shell is being fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. I was unaware of the precision, the narrowness of your question. But still I would like to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mortar makes three types of sounds. The shot, the shell being fired, that's one sound, and it has rather peculiar characteristics. The other sound is the sound made by the round on its descent; it's a whistling sound, a piercing sound. And the third sound is the moment when the shell actually explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at Mr. Higgs' report --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the same page in the English version. I would like the last page in the English version to be put on the screen, too. That's document P888. But the English version should -- we should go to the next page or ... I don't want to deal with charges. We have to move to the next page in the English version, page 14. I don't know what's going on. I would like to start with the words "At a range of only 900 metres ..." We're having some problems. Then it should be the previous page in the English version, the last sentence here where it reads: "At a range of only 900 metres ..." In the English version that's the last paragraph, and in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please look at it. "At a range of only 900 metres would put the firing position inside the confrontation line," and in the end, "At this distance they would have heard the round being fired, the observers would have heard it." Would they have heard it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we go to the next page in the English version, but just in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "At a range of 1.600 metres places the firing point in the area of the confrontation line but still in easy earshot of the UN observers." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "At a range of 2.400 metres puts the firing position in the hills, which is out of earshot of the UN observers due to the lay of the land. In other words, they would not have heard the round being fired due to the hills and valleys." My question to you is: If they could have heard it well, easily, at a range of 1.600 metres, is it possible that if the shell had been fired only 800 metres further away that now all of a sudden this sound could not be heard by a person with average hearing, with the most average of hearings?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: They should have heard the sound at that distance, too, quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it possible that one would not be able to hear the sound of five shells, provided they were all fired from a distance of about 2.400 metres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hesitate because I'm not entirely sure. The question seems to suggest that the four other shells, as is the evidence in this case, were fired from the same -- along the same direction that the shell that the Prosecution alleges was fired from that hit the marketplace. So I'm just attempting to inquire whether Mr. Tapuskovic is, in that question, asserting that the four other shells were fired along that same direction of fire, because, Mr. President, in the evidence in this case, our position is that the four other shells were fired from a direction of 220 to 240 degrees, which is some distance away from where the UN observers were, along the line towards Trebevic mountain. So I'm not sure if that question accurately reflects the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your intention here, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sachdeva was right, I was not specific enough. But what I intend, Your Honour, is to ask the witness, regardless of the position where the shell was fired, not hearing the shell being fired or four more shells. I'm not going into where the shell was fired from at all. I'm just talking about the possibility that the UN observers had not heard it being fired. I'm not going into the direction of fire or the place from which it was fired, so if it was fired from a distance of about 5 to 6 kilometres or 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To Judge Harhoff's question you said that there were three types of sound made by a mortar. Let us deal with the actual flight now. In which stage of the flight can one hear a projectile flying through the air?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Since a 120-millimetre projectile follows a parabolic pattern, we can hear the sound during the descending part of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've just described that sound for Judge Harhoff a few moments ago; therefore, I won't go back to that. But tell me this: Such a sound of such nature, is it also something that an average person can easily hear?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The characteristics of a projectile flight in its descent is such that one can hear the whistling sound 2 to 3 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what phase?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: During the descent. The closer to the ground --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You've given us an answer. Tell Their Honours this: Let us assume that a projectile was fired, for example, from a distance of 2.400 metres. What is the length of the flight measuring from the place of origin of fire, or rather, what is the duration and length of ascent as opposed to descent?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That can vary. As for that distance, an average trajectory would be about 2.500 metres. The descending phase would be about -- or rather, the descending phase is 2.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is telling me that the apex of the trajectory is also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the ascending trajectory up to the apex is 2.5 kilometres and the descending part of the trajectory is also 2.5 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As the projectile is falling down it can be heard. Can you tell Their Honours, can you describe for them the nature of that sound as of what moment when it leaves the apex and starts descending towards the target?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that it's a whistling sound. The closer the projectile is to the ground, the louder the intensity. And it is at its loudest just prior to hitting the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it's possible at all to say how long in terms of time it takes to leave the apex and hit the target?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the range and the distance and the charge, it can be anywhere between 20 seconds and as much as a full minute, 60 seconds, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm interested in the period of flight during which you can hear it.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That is one half of the entire flight time, that is, 15 to 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. When I ask you about the descending stage, tell me about the descending stage. So it's 15 to 20 seconds?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did I ask you this: If there were five shots fired from different sides from a distance of 2.5 kilometres, is it possible that not a single projectile would be heard? Is it possible that no projectile would be heard, although each projectile would have the descending pattern which lasts for 15 to 20 seconds?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What can be registered on the instruments which are custom-made in order to follow the sound of firing, flight, and impact? First of all, what is registered on the instruments which are supposed to follow the firing -- they're supposed to follow the sound of firing?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: In modern armies there are instruments which can follow sound. They can observe two types of sound - the sound of firing and the sound of explosion. In this case there are instruments which can register the moment of firing, they can register the sound that occurs, and based on certain mathematical calculation, according to that, one can determine the very source of sound, or rather, the place of origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Such instruments --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait, wait. At what distance from the origin of fire can such instrument register a firing?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: They can register the sound and they can do that at a distance up to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How much later after such an instrument has registered the sound those who work with that instrument, how much later would they be able to ascertain the actual firing position?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: One minute at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: If we have a trained crew with a good instrument and its characteristics are such that it takes the crew only one minute by using the information to determine the source of sound, and they can calculate the coordinates from which the shot occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we must take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garovic, before the break we were discussing the mortar sound, the sound of a round in flight. We talked about one projectile. What if there were five projectiles which were fired from approximately the same distance but from different locations? Would such instruments register the sound of impact of those projectiles?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Sound reconnaissance devices are made in such a way so as to be able to register the firing, the shot, and then in that case they must have registered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, these instruments do not register the sound of a round in flight but rather the sound coming from the place of fire.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the degree of accuracy in terms of pinpointing the exact location, and what is the reliability of such instruments?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Such instruments are so precise that the circular error is up to 10 metres. Such data is always considered accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested, first and foremost, at the very location from which a shell was fired. Can such an instrument determine the very point of firing with a possible error of up to 10 metres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell Their Honours if there is a chance of a radar device registering a 120-millimetre projectile?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: In modern armies there are radar devices which detect the place of firing of a mortar round as well. In this case it would be the Cymbeline radar device. Based on detecting the ascending pattern of the projectile, it can determine the place of firing with a degree of accuracy of plus or minus 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Provided a projectile was fired from a distance of 2.400 metres, you told us what would be the duration of the ascending stage and, from the apex, the descending part of the curve. What can be registered by this radar device as regards the curve which consists of an ascending and a descending stage?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: That radar device registers the ascending phase of the curve and it registers the projectile itself. It records it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that the ascending part of the curve from the distance of 2.400 metres is approximately 2.5 kilometres, does that mean that the radar registers the ascending part of the path up to that height?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The radar needn't register the entire curve of 2.500 metres. It only records the part of the flight pattern from the nozzle up to 200 metres away. This suffices, and based on that information, can calculates the entire curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you sketch that for us so that the Judges would be able to understand better what is the range that such a radar can detect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the earlier ruling. However, the opinions with respect to radars is somewhat different to the use of observers and traces left by mortars. And it's not that the Prosecution would not anticipate the issue with respect to radars and Cymbeline. However, when an expert comes and gives opinions and conclusions on the day that the expert is testifying without it being included in the report, it can leave the Prosecution in somewhat of a difficult position in terms of cross-examining the witness on these conclusions. The radar and Cymbeline issue is a very, very technical aspect that really, in my submission, should have been included in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your expertise in the matter of radars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an artillery officer, I was trained to use the SNR radars. With a long teaching career, I also became familiar in lecturing on radars to our cadets. However, we did not go into the very essentials and construction of the device, but we did study its use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what do you say about the objection? It seems to me that there are two matters. First, that this subject matter is not in the report. In my earlier ruling I said if it arose naturally from the expertise of the witness' report, then I would allow evidence to be given on it as something which is naturally incidental. I am not certain that this qualifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a very important issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That really was two issues in one. One, the subject matter being discussed is not in the report. And secondly, it's a different area from the expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the first issue, at page 21 - that's the English version 14 - the witness discussed Cymbeline radar systems. Well, you've given us your view about the earlier objection raised by Mr. Sachdeva. I will not go back to it. He is not an expert for radars, but he does know a few basic things. So I'm not insisting on expert aspects as regards radars but the elements that every artillery officer is aware of regarding the use of radars, because without such knowledge they cannot perform their job at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I do see it in the report, but it's really just a mention of the Cymbeline satellite radar systems. It doesn't go into any detail. There's nothing there to suggest to me that he possesses any knowledge, specialised knowledge in that area. But taking into account all these points, I'm going to allow the evidence to be given on the basis that there is mention of it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garovic, to the extent that you know about some basic things, what you began to draw here, this pertains to the -- what happens here in this area that -- in this thing that you just started drawing for us?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The Cymbeline radar is set at such a spot that the radar beams cover the area where mortars are expected to operate. At the moment when a shell is fired, at the height of about 200 to 300 metres, the radar beams register the entry of the shell into the beams and registered the bear coordinates. And then at a higher part of the trajectory, 300 to 400 metres - that depends on the settings of the radar - another recording is taken of the same shell at a different height and the parameters are recorded. Then a calculation is made, the parameters are processed, and the coordinates are established on the basis of the ascent of the impact. The source of the projectile is determined. The circular error is up to 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from the fact that the radar is able to establish with unerring accuracy the point from which the shell was fired, what else is the radar able to establish with unerring accuracy?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The speed of the flight over a certain area which serves to determine the charge used to fire the round.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? In addition to determining the spot, the radar can also determine the charge that was used?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for a radar such as this one not to register a single ascent of a shell fired from any mortar, including the mortars at such a range from any direction, from the position where theoretically we could say that a shell was fired 2.500 metres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Since I had Cymbeline radars in my unit - we had a unit that worked with those radars - it is impossible for a shell to be fired without the radar registering the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this respect does it matter at all, although you have already answered this question, if the length of the trajectory is 2.500 metres, which as you indicated, is the case in mortars firing a shell from a distance of 2.400 metres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter at all because the radar records the trajectory up to the height of a maximum of 400 metres - interpreter's correction: 1000 metres - to determine the charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now please tell me: If you have a person with the average hearing, such as the UN observers have, if they failed to register the firing, if an average human hearing, such as the observers of the United Nations possess, if it failed to register the sound of the flight of the round, if this was not registered by the state-of-the-art device monitoring the sound of the firing of the shell, if no radar system, the radar system that you mentioned, or any other that is even more advanced failed to register the trajectory of the shell, and if only one thing was heard in all this, if only one thing was heard, the impact, the sound at the place where a shell landed, can you explain that in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the conditions that you just explained to us, the sound of the explosion of a body can only be heard if such a device was exploded in static conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should move on to another topic. In chapter 2 of your report, that's paragraph 18, or rather, page 18 in the B/C/S version, which would be page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no reason for it to be shown to the witness, or perhaps we should.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that page you spoke about -- you spoke about craters. What I want to ask you before showing you anything: A crater caused by a 120-millimetre mortar, can it in itself provide accurate parameters or elements to determine the direction and the range from which this shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A crater caused by a shell, a 120-millimetre mortar shell, cannot give a single accurate parameter to determine any of the elements of the trajectory or anything that would indicate the place from which the shell was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At page 18 in the B/C/S version - that's page 12 in the English version - and now I have to waste some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document DD00-4582.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's your report. I can't find it now exactly, but that's the passage starting with the word "The diameter and depth..." That's at page 12 in the English version, the last paragraph. Could you please look at the B/C/S version, that would be the second paragraph right in the middle. It says: "The funnel of the crater, the edges and epicentre of the explosion crater which would allow for a precise determination of reference points required for taking reliable and precise measurements are not well-defined." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me whether this applies to every crater regardless of the type of the mortar, including the 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if a shell landed on the same type of ground. If you have loose soil, the crater is different. Its depth is different. It can be even wider because of the nature of the soil, the firmness of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why is that so, in addition to what you just told us? Why is it difficult? Could you explain this to us more precisely, at least to a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: When a shell hits the ground, earth or soil, because the soil is soft, it penetrates deeper into the ground and it ejects a larger quantity of soil out of the explosion site. That's why the crater is deeper and it is larger, because more soil had been ejected. If the shell hits a concrete or asphalt, because this ground is firm, the shell does not penetrate into the ground at all, but all the traces are based on the -- all the traces are those of the gunpowder gases that were ejected at the moment of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But even if a shell hits a firmer ground, it leaves a funnel-shaped crater behind.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's much shallower. It penetrates to a very shallow degree. The funnel is very shallow, unlike when it hits loose soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But what determines the length of the funnel? Don't talk to me about soil. Tell me about firmer ground, asphalt, concrete. How deep would the funnel be, and what would the depth depend on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: When a shell hits firmer ground, the funnel is shallow and the depth of the funnel indicates the speed of the shell before the explosion itself. So the only thing that could be read from the depth of the funnel is the impact velocity at the time of the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't seem to be able to answer my question. What does the depth depend on? You say that it's shallow, but what would the depth of the funnel depend, 1, 2, 5 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: I did say that the depth would depend on the velocity the shell had at the moment of impact and the weight of the shell. That's what it depends on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what does the speed, the velocity, depend on?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The velocity, I apologise. The velocity of the shell would depend on the charge that was used to fire it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many charges would a 120-millimetre shell have?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A 120-millimetre shell has the base charge used to fire it and six additional charge -- the base charge that is not used to fire it and six additional charges that are used to actually fire it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in this case, because you were telling us that radars are able to determine the type of charge, in fact did you have any elements here that you could use to determine the type of charge?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the crater it is impossible to determine any indicators that would tell us what type of charge was used to fire that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you at least tell the Judges, depending on the depth of the funnel, what could you tell on the basis of that? What kind of charge was used, at least approximately?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the depth of the funnel, one can assume the charge that was used when the round was fired. The deeper the funnel, the stronger the charge. If the shell was fired using the first or the second charges, then the funnel is at its shallowest, maybe 1 or 2 centimetres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I show you anything else, could you please tell us, what can you conclude on the basis of the traces left by the shrapnel caused by the explosion of a 120-millimetre round hitting an asphalt or concrete surface?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Two things could be observed in the crater: The funnel and a band of shrapnel, fragments, shell fragments, around the crater. On the basis of this band, the general direction from which the shell had come can be determined and the angle of impact at the moment of impact or explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in what relations? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in what relations could this be determined?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of these two parameters. With the epicentre of the funnel and the shrapnel band, one can determine the approximate angle of descent and the direction from which the shell had come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in general, approximate direction.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Of what assistance -- you spoke about that in your report. You spoke about the magnetic compass. Let me not go back to it. At any rate, can we, first of all, say that apart from the general direction, the general characteristics of the crater, the depth and the shrapnel marks, do they make it possible for us to determine the position from which the round was fired?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Based on those parameters it is not possible to determine the place from which the round was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And would the use of a magnetic compass?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A hand-held compass that was used when investigating the incidents, well, with that device one can calculate an approximate direction from which the projectile had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 19 of your report. In the English, it is page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems the system is down. We are unable to use the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so? The court deputy is carrying out a check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we wait for the technician to come, could I take some time just to ask a few clarifying questions to the witness. I mean, we will compensate you for the Bench's questions in the end, Mr. Tapuskovic. But speaking of the craters of the mortars, I understand you to say that the depth of the funnel depends only on the velocity of the shell and the weight of the shell, and that raises the question: What about the explosion itself? Does that leave any impact in the funnel of the crater, or is it only the velocity and the weight that will leave an impact on the soil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said is correct. It depends on the velocity, since at the moment of impact and between that moment and the explosion itself, this is the period during which the projectile penetrates the ground. At that time the soil is ejected and the crater is deeper. Therefore, it is not only the velocity but the velocity at the moment before the impact because that increases the size of the funnel. The lesser the speed, the less penetration of the projectile and the smaller the crater. However, there is an explosion in both cases. With projectiles, which can be made to slow down when using the ignition mechanism, the penetration is greater; therefore, the depth of the crater and the amount of ejected earth is greater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. This is very useful. Another question that we have come across in this case is the position of the tail-fin. We have understood that under certain circumstances the tail-fin is found in the crater itself and in other circumstances the tail-fin is ejected and thrown away and can be found away from the crater. Could you explain to us under which conditions a tail-fin is normally to be found in the crater itself? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not difficult. I'm a teacher and I can reply to your question. The stabiliser or the tail of the projectile is the same speed as the projectile itself. At the moment of explosion it is ejected. The speed at which it is ejected depends on the speed of flight before the impact and the explosive charge. Since the projectile has constant values, the ejection is constant as well; however, the speed affects the ejection of the tail-fin and that also has impact on how far it will be from the place of impact. In my 40-year-long career I did not come across a tail-fin which would be in the very centre of the crater. Usually and most often it is at the edge of the crater or a few metres away, say, 5 or 6. That depends on the speed. For the tail-fin to actually penetrate the centre of explosion, it needs to have a very great initial speed; however, such projectiles have the speed of 3 to 400 metres per second before impact and the speed of penetration of the tail-fin would have to be over 700 metres per second, which means that such a tail-fin has no required speed at which it could actually penetrate the very place of impact. The tail-fin is always around the crater, closer or a bit further away, but never in the epicentre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Judge Harhoff. This actually spared some of my time. Otherwise, I would have had to ask the same question. I don't know whether the system is up now. It's still not there, but I think I can continue examining the witness nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not necessarily important for you to be able to see what's in the report. When drafting the report you mentioned a compass, a hand-held compass --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the crater in itself can provide us with certain data on the direction. What about a hand-held compass as used by people who were in the area of combat? What can that device tell us? What can it tell us out of the entire range of things that are essential in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: A hand-held compass is an instrument used by our units, usually the artillery units, but it only determines the general direction of the azimuth and is used for a general navigation of soldiers and officers in open space. Precise measurements with a hand-held compass are not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A hand-held compass of such possibility, with the help of the elements that can be deducted from the shape and depth of the crater, what sort of reliability can such data in total give us? So judging by the elements discernible from the crater and what the compass tells us, how can that help us in making certain conclusions as to the origin of fire, if we don't know what the charge was?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: Based on such parameters as mentioned a minute ago, one can only give unreliable and approximate data on the direction from which the shell had come. Therefore, we're not discussing the place from which it was fired but rather the direction from which it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on on the issue of the compass, I wanted to ask you this: The hand-held compass as such, does anything impact its operation in the field as to its general ability?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The hand-held compass is an instrument using a magnetic needle to provide measurements. In certain conditions in which close to the place of inspection there are sources of magnetic radiation, if there is lots of metal and so on and so forth, the hand-held compass will not provide us with even remotely accurate data, and as such it cannot be used even in the most general sense. It is almost 100 per cent unreliable in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we are in an urban setting, in the centre of any town in the world, where there's plenty of metal - maybe there's no weaponry close by but other metal objects - to what degree does that affect the operation of the compass?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC
utterances.text: The operation of a compass in an urban setting is practically excluded because of the electrical power lines, metal piles and pylons, railroad wagons, and so on and so forth. All that has a great impact on its ability to calculate the azimuth and direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
